assets.topic: Purpose Maximization vs. Profit Maximization vs. Checklist Ethics
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen sorting board glows in three columns, each labeled with one operating system or approach: purpose maximization, profit maximization, and checklist compliance. Small orange evidence tiles — a shoe icon for TOMS, a stat card reading 800 million, a gavel for compliance rulings — hover as the player drags each one into its column.
assets.player_mission: Read each evidence tile about real companies, pledges, and policies, then drag it into the column it best matches. Place at least 5 of 6 tiles correctly to pass the audit screen.
key_concepts: Motivation 3.0 does not reject profits but places equal emphasis on purpose maximization.
TOMS Shoes describes itself as a for-profit company with giving at its core, launched by Blake Mycoskie in 2006.
Motivation 2.0 relegates purpose to the status of an ornament that must not get in the way of profits.
Gary Hamel argues that wealth maximization lacks the power to fully mobilize human energies.
Worldwide co-op membership doubled to 800 million people in the last three decades, per writer Marjorie Kelly.
Purpose provides activation energy for living, according to psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi.
The MBA Oath is a voluntary code of conduct pledging managers to serve the greater good.
Ethics guidelines can unintentionally move purposeful behavior from Type I to Type X when reduced to checklists.
Max Bazerman observed that weak ethical standards turn doing the right thing into checking off boxes.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests self-determination theory's claim that purpose is a basic source of activation: people perform and persist best when their goals serve a cause larger than themselves. Pink's evidence is the divergence between falling compensated engagement and rising volunteerism, showing purpose nourishes people in ways pay alone does not.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.question: Classify each organizational impulse below. Specifically, where does the TOMS Shoes model — a for-profit company with giving at its core — belong?

rows.label: TOMS Shoes sells a pair and gives a pair away, calling itself a for-profit company with giving at its core
Gary Hamel: as an emotional catalyst, wealth maximization lacks the power to fully mobilize human energies
A firm reduces affirmative action to a list of requirements to prove it isn't discriminating
The MBA Oath pledges managers to serve the greater good rather than only the bottom line
Worldwide co-op membership doubled to 800 million people over roughly three decades
Bazerman's warning: a weak set of ethical standards turns doing the right thing into checking off boxes

distractors: b — TOMS is simply a charity that finances its operations through shoe sales
c — TOMS must meet ethics checklists so it won't get sued or fined
a — but only because TOMS chases profit and treats giving as a marketing ornament
assets.explanation: TOMS is neither a pure charity nor a profit-first business: Pink describes it as a for-profit company with giving at its core, the hallmark of purpose maximization, where purpose is the objective and profit is the catalyst. Checklist ethics sorts to column C because it shifts workers from intrinsic motivation to box-checking for legal safety, and Hamel's remark anchors the Motivation 2.0 view that wealth maximization cannot mobilize human energies.

assets.topic: The Good Life: Purpose Goals vs. Profit Goals at Rochester
assets.visual_frame_description: A college quad at sunset with a graduation cap floating above the gates. Two dossier cards labeled Profit Goals and Purpose Goals unfold on screen, each with a happiness meter that slides in opposite directions as the player inspects the follow-up data.
assets.player_mission: Classify each graduate aspiration as intrinsic, extrinsic, or neutral, then identify which goal profile the Rochester study found to increase anxiety and depression even when attained.
key_concepts: Deci, Ryan, and Niemiec surveyed Rochester seniors about their life goals and followed up one to two years into their careers.
Extrinsic aspirations include becoming wealthy or achieving fame; Pink calls them profit goals.
Intrinsic aspirations include helping others improve their lives, learning, and growing; Pink calls them purpose goals.
Purpose-goal attainers reported higher satisfaction and subjective well-being than when they were in college.
Profit-goal attainers reported satisfaction, self-esteem, and positive affect no higher than when they were students.
Profit-goal attainers showed increases in anxiety, depression, and other negative indicators.
The researchers concluded that attainment of profit goals has no impact on well-being and actually contributes to ill-being.
Richard Ryan noted that profit-goal high attainers are busy making money, leaving less room for love, attention, caring, and empathy.
Satisfaction depends not merely on having goals, but on having the right goals.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests self-determination theory's distinction between extrinsic and intrinsic aspirations: attaining material goals fails to lift well-being and can worsen it. The longitudinal Rochester study found purpose-goal attainers happier and less anxious while profit-goal attainers were worse off despite reaching their goals.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.question: Deci, Ryan, and Niemiec tracked University of Rochester graduates one to two years into their careers. Which aspiration profile showed rises in anxiety and depression even while attaining its goals?

rows.label: A graduate wants to help others improve their lives
A graduate wants to become wealthy
A graduate wants to achieve fame
Attainers of these goals reported satisfaction no higher than when they were students
Attainers reported higher subjective well-being and quite low anxiety and depression
A graduate wants to learn and grow
Attainers showed increases in anxiety and depression even while attaining their goals

distractors: a — purpose goals raised anxiety and depression in the follow-up data
c — both profiles showed identical well-being after attainment
b — but only among students who failed to attain their goals
assets.explanation: The Rochester follow-up found that graduates with extrinsic aspirations (wealth, fame) who attained their goals reported satisfaction, self-esteem, and positive affect no higher than in college — and showed more anxiety and depression, so attaining profit goals contributed to ill-being. Purpose-goal attainers, by contrast, reported higher well-being and low anxiety, which is why those rows sort to column A and the target row to column B.

assets.topic: Three Realms of the Purpose Motive: Goals, Words, and Policies
assets.visual_frame_description: A three-chambered museum exhibit: Goal Hall shows shoe boxes multiplying into donations, Word Hall shows speech bubbles morphing into honest dialogue, and Policy Hall shows a wall calendar with one glowing day per week reserved for meaningful work.
assets.player_mission: Sort each example from the chapter into the realm where the purpose motive stirs first — goals, words, or policies — and pinpoint exactly where the Mayo Clinic experiment belongs.
key_concepts: The purpose motive first appears in three realms of organizational life: goals, words, and policies.
Physicians at the Mayo Clinic who spent one day a week on the aspect of their job most meaningful to them had half the burnout rate of those who did not.
Dunn and Norton propose shifting part of a company's charitable-giving budget so individual employees donate chosen sums.
Pro-social spending — spending money on other people or on a cause — can increase subjective well-being.
Sylvia Hewlett found that boomers and Gen Y are redefining success and accepting a radically remixed set of rewards.
Neither boomers nor Gen Y rate money as the most important form of compensation.
Robert Reich's pronoun test gauges organization health by whether employees refer to the company as we or they.
Gary Hamel says goals described as efficiency and advantage lack the power to rouse human hearts.
We companies and they companies are very different places, and in Motivation 3.0 we wins.
The MBA Oath urges managers to create value that no single individual can create alone.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario maps the purpose motive onto the three realms Pink identifies — goals, words, and policies — testing whether the learner can place the Mayo Clinic trial and pro-social giving in the policy realm rather than the goals realm. The evidence base spans Hewlett's generational research, pro-social spending studies, and the halved burnout finding at Mayo.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.question: Pink maps the early stirrings of the purpose motive onto three realms of organizational life. Where does the Mayo Clinic experiment — letting doctors spend one day a week on their most meaningful work — belong?
assets.column_a_label: Goals — remixed rewards and purpose maximizers
assets.column_b_label: Words — the purpose dialect in corporate language
assets.column_c_label: Policies — autonomy enlisted in service of purpose

rows.label: TOMS Shoes' give-one-for-one business model
The MBA Oath's opening pledge to serve the greater good
The Mayo Clinic trial letting doctors spend one day a week on the most meaningful part of the job
Dunn and Norton's proposal that employees be given sums to donate to charities they choose
Sylvia Hewlett's finding that Gen Y wants a great team and the ability to give back to society
Hamel's call to infuse mundane business activities with honor, truth, love, justice, and beauty
Robert Reich's pronoun test — listening for we versus they

distractors: a — it is a goals shift like the TOMS model
b — it is a words shift like the MBA Oath
c — but only for physicians, not as a model other organizations could adopt
assets.explanation: The Mayo Clinic field trial is a policy: deliberately restructuring work time so physicians spend a day a week on the aspect of the job most meaningful to them, cutting burnout in half — Pink calls it 20 percent time with a purpose. TOMS and the Gen Y remixed rewards belong to the goals realm, while the MBA Oath, Hamel's vocabulary, and Reich's pronoun test belong to the words realm.

assets.topic: The Purpose Motive and the Type I Tripod
assets.visual_frame_description: A boardroom with two glowing pitch decks on opposite walls: one covered in bar charts and margin curves, the other showing a map of small towns dotted with building icons. Warren, the sixty-two-year-old CEO, leans back in a leather chair while a third screen shows a slogan factory stamping words.
assets.player_mission: Choose which corporate plan actually carries the purpose motive, then defend that choice by redesigning the incentives and language so profit talk does not crowd purpose out of the firm.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: Purpose is the third leg of the Type I tripod: autonomy and mastery are essential, but purpose provides the context that lets the other two legs accomplish more. Autonomous people working toward mastery perform at very high levels, and those who do so in the service of some greater objective can achieve even more; Motivation 3.0 pursues purpose maximization while Motivation 2.0 treated purpose as an ornament.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are a strategy consultant at a retreat for Harlow & Reed, a mid-sized engineering firm. Two teams pitch the next decade. Team Argus presents a financial plan to expand market share and lift margins by 12 percent, citing efficiency, advantage, and differentiation. Team Meridian presents a plan to anchor the firm's work in rebuilding public infrastructure for underserved towns, promising steady profit as a by-product. The CEO, Warren, says he is too old to chase butterflies.
assets.stage_1_question: Which plan best embodies what Pink calls the purpose motive?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Team Meridian's plan — it makes purpose the objective and treats profit as the catalyst or happy by-product of attaining it, exactly the Motivation 3.0 stance in which purpose maximization, not profit maximization, supplies the activation energy.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The board accepts Meridian's pitch, but CFO Priya wants to incentivize the engineers with a 20-percent bonus pool tied to quarterly profit targets and a slogan wall reading Efficiency is honor. You have one edit to the implementation. What do you change?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Drop the profit-tied bonus and the slogan — profit-contingent if-then incentives and efficiency language push purpose back to ornament status and cannot mobilize human energies; instead, keep pay fair and out of the way and let engineers spend one day a week on the community projects, following the Mayo Clinic model of 20 percent time with a purpose.
key_concepts: Purpose is the third leg of the Type I tripod, providing context for autonomy and mastery.
Autonomous people working toward mastery perform at very high levels.
Those who work toward mastery in the service of a greater objective can achieve even more.
Motivation 2.0 relegated purpose to the status of an ornament.
Motivation 3.0 places equal emphasis on purpose maximization, without rejecting profits.
Gary Hamel: wealth maximization lacks the power to fully mobilize human energies.
The most deeply motivated people hitch their desires to a cause larger than themselves.
At the Mayo Clinic, one day a week on meaningful work halved physician burnout.
Compensated engagement is falling while volunteerism is rising in the United States.
Volunteer work is nourishing people in ways that paid work simply does not.
assets.theory_summary: The battle tests self-determination theory's claim that purpose, alongside autonomy and mastery, is a core need that supplies activation energy for high performance. Pink's evidence is the boomers' demographic surge of purpose-seeking, rising volunteerism, and the Mayo Clinic burnout finding — though the broad social sweep is his synthesis rather than a single controlled experiment.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.topic: TOMS Shoes and the Rise of Purpose Maximizers
assets.visual_frame_description: A sunlit storefront where canvas flat-soled shoes are stacked on crates beside a world map dotted with delivery pins. A scale floats above the counter, one pan holding a new shoe and the other holding a child's sneaker, balanced perfectly.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose what kind of enterprise TOMS is in Pink's framework, then defend its giving-at-the-core model against a private-equity deal that would downgrade giving to an ornament.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: Purpose maximizers are operations that make purpose the goal and profit the catalyst rather than the objective: for-profit companies with giving at their core, B corporations, and cooperatives. Pink argues such ventures are so incompatible with Motivation 2.0 logic that they would seize up and crash under that operating system.
assets.stage_1_observation: Step into a bright storefront in the summer of 2006. Blake Mycoskie has just launched TOMS Shoes: hip, canvas, flat-soled shoes on display beside a wall chart showing that every purchase ships a second pair to a child in a developing country. A shopper asks the clerk: Is this a charity that sells shoes, or a business that gives shoes away?
assets.stage_1_question: How does Pink classify ventures like TOMS?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: TOMS is neither simply a charity nor a conventional profit-maximizing business — the company itself answers that it is both and describes itself as a for-profit company with giving at its core, a purpose maximizer where purpose is the goal and profit is the catalyst.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Two years later, a private-equity investor offers Mycoskie a deal: double margins by dropping the give-one model to one pair per ten sold and rebrand the donation as an annual charity event. He gives you one recommendation to deliver.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Turn the offer down — cutting giving into a box-ticking annual event turns purpose into an ornament, exactly the move that would flatten TOMS into the socially responsible but rarely delivering template Pink criticizes; the venture's identity depends on purpose remaining at the core of every sale.
key_concepts: Blake Mycoskie launched TOMS Shoes in 2006.
Every time TOMS sells a pair of shoes, it gives away another pair to a child in a developing country.
TOMS describes itself as a for-profit company with giving at its core.
TOMS is neither a charity that finances itself with shoe sales nor a business that sacrifices earnings to do good — it is both.
Purpose maximizers pursue purpose and use profit as the catalyst rather than the objective.
B corporations, for-benefit organizations, and low-profit LLCs recast the goals of the traditional business enterprise.
Worldwide co-op membership doubled to 800 million people over three decades.
Not-only-for-profit enterprises differ from the socially responsible businesses that have rarely delivered on their promise.
Under Motivation 2.0 logic, a venture like TOMS would seize up and crash.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the purpose motive: organizations that put giving at the core of the business model rather than as a side program. Pink's evidence is TOMS, the surge of co-ops and benefit corporations, and the demographic shift of boomers and Gen Y toward remixed, nonmonetary rewards — a popular-science synthesis of emerging business trends.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.topic: Checklist Ethics vs. Autonomy in Service of Purpose
assets.visual_frame_description: A desk with a laminated 40-item ethics checklist beside a glass jar overflowing with folded donation cards and a small sign reading Your 200 dollars, your pick. Overhead, a graph splits into a red falling line labeled intrinsic and a green rising line labeled satisfaction.
assets.player_mission: Predict the motivational side effect of a compliance checklist, then pick the single policy that converts the credit union from box-checking back to purpose-driven giving.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: Corporate ethics guidelines, however well-intentioned, can backfire: by giving people a fairly weak set of standards to meet, they replace intrinsic motivation — do it because it's right — with extrinsic box-checking — make sure we don't get sued or fined. Bazerman's warning is that compliance can crowd out purpose, and the better path is enlisting autonomy in the service of purpose maximization.
assets.stage_1_observation: At Verano Credit Union, a loan officer scandal has just hit the local news. General counsel Denise drafts a 40-item ethics checklist, mandating quarterly sign-offs and compliance training for every employee. You watch Dana, a conscientious loan officer who once refused a bonus for pushing a risky product, spend her Friday reading the checklist aloud and asking peers whether each item counts.
assets.stage_1_question: What does Max Bazerman's analysis predict about Dana's motivation after the checklist arrives?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Her motivation shifts from intrinsic to extrinsic: instead of doing the right thing because it is right, she now meets the minimal ethical standard to avoid punishment, because the guidelines handed her an alternate set of standards — do this so you can check off all these boxes.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Denise wants to restore the credit union's moral energy and asks you to pick one lever: (a) double the checklist items and add fines for missed sign-offs; (b) give each employee a 200-dollar budget each quarter to donate to any cause they choose; (c) pay a compliance bonus for perfect sign-off records. Which lever do you choose?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Choose the donation budget — Dunn and Norton's pro-social spending research shows that handing employees control over how the organization gives back improves their satisfaction, which is exactly the model of enlisting autonomy in the service of purpose instead of adding another layer of extrinsic control.
key_concepts: Corporate ethics guidelines can unintentionally move purposeful behavior out of the Type I schema and into Type X.
Bazerman: giving people a weak set of ethical standards replaces doing it because it's right with checking off all these boxes.
Checklist ethics can turn affirmative action into a set of requirements to show the organization isn't discriminating.
Workers may meet the minimal ethical standards to avoid punishment while the guidelines inject no purpose.
The better approach is to enlist the power of autonomy in the service of purpose maximization.
The correlation between money and happiness is weak past a certain, quite modest level.
Pro-social spending — on other people or on a cause — can increase subjective well-being.
Dunn and Norton propose giving employees sums to donate to the charities of their choice.
Handing employees control over corporate giving may do more for satisfaction than another if-then financial incentive.
Instances of unethical behavior have not declined despite years of crafting corporate ethics guidelines.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests self-determination theory's crowding-out effect: extrinsic standards displace intrinsic moral motivation, a mechanism Bazerman describes in the book. The corrective per Pink is autonomy in service of purpose, supported by Aknin, Dunn, and Norton's pro-social spending findings that giving employees control over charitable dollars raises well-being.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.topic: What Happens When You Attain Profit Goals
assets.visual_frame_description: A quiet coaching session in a glass-walled office at an accounting firm: Marcus, twenty-six, sits across from Priya the leadership coach while Sana, a nonprofit auditor, leans in from a side chair. A subtle on-screen graph shows two happiness curves crossing in opposite directions as the conversation unfolds.
assets.player_mission: Coach Marcus through the paradox of attaining profit goals without gaining happiness — use the Rochester study and Ryan's explanation to redirect his ambition toward purpose goals without abandoning his ambition.
assets.scenario_setup: You are Priya, a leadership coach at a Big Four accounting firm. Twenty-six-year-old senior analyst Marcus just made partner track with a six-figure raise and booked a session to figure out why he feels hollow. Across the room, his colleague Sana, who took a lower-paying role at a nonprofit audit shop, reports feeling more alive than ever. Your goal is to help Marcus read his own results with self-determination theory — and keep him from doubling down on the wrong goal.
dialogue: Marcus: I hit the numbers. One-eighty hours of billable work this month, top-bracket bonus, name on the partner list. And I feel... nothing. What is wrong with me?

Priya: Nothing is wrong with you. A University of Rochester study followed graduates one to two years into their careers — people who attained their wealth and fame goals weren't any happier than they were in college.
Marcus: So I should make more money? Maybe the goal was just too small.
Sana: I make half of what you do, Marcus. But I audited a school district's books and they got laptops for every classroom. I sleep better.

Priya: That's the striking part of the research — profit-goal attainers showed increases in anxiety and depression, even while winning. Richard Ryan's explanation: they're busy making money and attending to themselves, leaving less room for love, attention, caring, and the things that truly count.
Marcus: So what do I put in the goals column instead? I can't exactly write feel good on a performance review.

Priya: Stay ambitious — but hitch the ambition to purpose goals: helping others, learning, growing. The study found purpose-goal attainers reported higher satisfaction and lower anxiety than in college.
Sana: Try this: before your next raise conversation, ask what a cause larger than yourself would have you build. Then let that sentence steer the work.
choices: Tell Marcus to keep the money but redirect his drive: keep one day a week for meaningful work, and set a purpose goal alongside the profit goal.
Agree that the goal was too small and advise doubling the targets — more money and a bigger title will finally scratch the itch.
Suggest Marcus quietly transfer to Sana's nonprofit firm so he can escape profit goals entirely.
Advise Marcus to separate his feelings from his career — feelings are unreliable, but the bonus is real.
assets.theoretical_principle: Intrinsic versus extrinsic aspirations (Deci, Ryan, and Niemiec)
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 works because it keeps the attained profit goal harmless while adding intrinsic aspirations: the Rochester follow-up found purpose-goal attainers reported higher satisfaction and lower anxiety, while profit-goal attainers were worse off even when successful. Choice 1 is the trap Ryan describes — expanding the goal that is already failing, a road of further unhappiness mistaken for the road to happiness. Choice 2 abandons the autonomy Marcus clearly values in his work, and choice 3 discounts real subjective evidence, which is exactly how high attainers wind up with the ill-being the research documented.
key_concepts: Deci and Ryan's Rochester follow-up tracked graduates one to two years after college.
Extrinsic aspirations seek wealth and fame; Pink calls these profit goals.
Intrinsic aspirations seek to help others, learn, and grow; Pink calls these purpose goals.
Attaining profit goals did not raise satisfaction, self-esteem, or positive affect.
Profit-goal attainers showed increases in anxiety, depression, and other negative indicators.
Purpose-goal attainers reported higher subjective well-being and low anxiety and depression.
Richard Ryan: high profit-goal attainers are busy making money, leaving less room for love, attention, caring, and empathy.
Satisfaction depends on having the right goals, not merely on having goals.
Chasing more money after attaining profit goals can drive people down a road of further unhappiness.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests self-determination theory's aspiration distinction: attaining extrinsic goals fails to improve well-being and can worsen it, while intrinsic aspirations support it. The Rochester follow-up and Ryan's empathy explanation ground the coaching advice the player must deliver.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.topic: Words and Policies: Keeping Volunteerism Alive
assets.visual_frame_description: An executive office at Pillar Health where CEO Greta gestures at a chart of volunteer hours climbing steeply; Malik, the chief operating officer, holds a clipboard with the word mandate crossed out. A window shows employees heading out to a community garden on a Saturday.
assets.player_mission: Steer the CEO away from a mandatory volunteer program with sign-in sheets and promotion credit, and toward a purpose-preserving design that keeps volunteerism intrinsically motivated.
assets.scenario_setup: You are Malik, chief operating officer of Pillar Health, a 300-person insurance company. Employee volunteer participation has tripled this year — uncompensated effort is rising even as paid engagement surveys fall. CEO Greta sees an opportunity to formalize it: she wants a mandated four-hour monthly Community Service Block with sign-in sheets, credit toward promotion, and a compliance officer. Your mission is to steer the conversation so the policy does not extinguish the very intrinsic flame it aims to fan.
dialogue: Greta: Malik, great news — volunteerism is through the roof. Let's institutionalize it: four mandatory hours a month, sign-in sheets, and it counts toward your promotion rubric.
Malik: Slow down. The rising volunteer line in our data is nourishing people precisely because paid work isn't. If we make it an obligation, we hand people an alternate set of standards to check off.
Greta: But how do we scale good deeds without structure? Where's the accountability?

Malik: Bazerman's caution cuts both ways: give people a weak set of standards to meet and they stop asking what's right and start asking what's required. We would convert intrinsic motivation into extrinsic motivation.
Greta: Fine — then what does a purpose-conscious policy actually look like?

Malik: Give people control. Earmark a giving budget and let each employee donate their share to any cause they choose, the way Dunn and Norton suggest. Or let teams pick their own volunteer projects and their own time.
Greta: Hmm. And the promotion credit?

Malik: Drop it. The moment volunteerism feeds the bonus calculus it becomes another if-then reward. The Mayo Clinic found letting people spend one day a week on what matters halved burnout — that's the direction of travel.
choices: Propose replacing the mandate with a per-employee donation budget and self-chosen volunteer projects, with no sign-in sheets and no promotion credit.
Support the mandate but soften the optics: call it an opportunity and keep the sign-in sheets quietly.
Compromise at two mandatory hours a month with a small community stars badge system to keep morale up.
Advise Greta to drop volunteering as a company matter entirely — volunteers will keep doing it anyway.
assets.theoretical_principle: Autonomy in service of purpose maximization (the crowding-out effect)
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 preserves what the science says volunteers are feeding on — self-direction and a cause larger than themselves — while adding pro-social control that, per Dunn and Norton, raises well-being. Choices 1 and 2 smuggle extrinsic contingencies in the back door, recreating the box-checking that Bazerman warns turns doing the right thing into checking off boxes. Choice 3 abandons organizational support entirely, forfeiting the policies realm where purpose can be scaled beyond individual effort.
key_concepts: Employee volunteerism is rising in the United States even as compensated engagement falls.
Volunteer work is nourishing people in ways that paid work simply does not.
Motivation 2.0 does not recognize purpose as a motivator.
Ethics guidelines can unintentionally move purposeful behavior from Type I into Type X.
Bazerman: weak ethical standards turn doing the right thing into checking off boxes.
Giving employees control over how the organization gives back can improve their satisfaction.
Dunn and Norton propose giving individual employees sums to donate to the charities of their choice.
The Mayo Clinic trial let physicians spend one day a week on the aspect of their job most meaningful to them.
Mayo Clinic doctors in the trial had half the burnout rate of those who did not participate.
Handing employees control over giving back may beat one more if-then financial incentive for satisfaction.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the crowding-out mechanism of self-determination theory: formalizing intrinsically rewarding activity with mandates converts it into extrinsic box-checking. The corrective is autonomy in service of purpose — Dunn and Norton's pro-social giving and the Mayo Clinic's purpose day, both presented in the chapter as purpose-centered policy.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

chapters.title: Type I for Individuals: Nine Strategies for Awakening Your Motivation

assets.topic: Flow Test, Oblique Cards, and Deliberate Practice
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory bench holds three instruments side by side: a pager buzzing at random intervals beside a notepad, a deck of black cards with cryptic phrases, and a stopwatch hovering over a practice schedule. Each instrument illuminates as the player classifies the evidence tiles.
assets.player_mission: Classify each technique described on the evidence tiles — the pager-based flow test, the Oblique Strategies deck, and deliberate practice — into its correct instrument column.
key_concepts: Csikszentmihalyi equipped research participants with electronic pagers to sample their mental states at random intervals.
The pager studies paged participants approximately eight times a day for a week.
Real-time reports proved far more honest and revealing than previous methods.
The flow test uses forty random reminders in a week, recording what you're doing, how you feel, and whether you're in flow.
Flow reports can reveal which times of day are most flow-friendly.
Oblique Strategies is a set of one hundred cards published by Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt in 1975.
Oblique cards contain a single, often inscrutable question or statement designed to push you out of a mental rut.
Deliberate practice has one objective: to improve performance, per Anders Ericsson.
Deliberate practice is mentally and physically exhausting, which is why so few people commit to it.
assets.theory_summary: The scenario contrasts three mastery tools from the book: experience sampling (the flow test), associative re-framing (Oblique cards), and structured skill-building (deliberate practice). Csikszentmihalyi's pager method stands out because it captures flow in real time rather than through memory, an evidence-based technique Pink recommends for discovering your true source of intrinsic motivation.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.question: Csikszentmihalyi's research team paged participants about eight times a day for a week, asking about their mental state at that moment. Which technique does the self-administered version — forty random checks in a week — belong to?

rows.label: Set a reminder to go off at forty random times in a week and record what you're doing and feeling
A card reading: Your mistake was a hidden intention
Shoot five hundred free throws rather than ten at the end of practice
Look for which times of day are more flow-friendly and restructure your day accordingly
Pull a card when you're stymied to push yourself out of a mental rut
Seek constant, critical feedback on your performance
Published by Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt in 1975 as a set of one hundred cards

distractors: b — the pager method comes from Eno and Schmidt
c — it is a deliberate-practice drill with five hundred repetitions
a — but only for athletes and artists, not knowledge workers
assets.explanation: The flow test is Csikszentmihalyi's methodological innovation: random real-time paging turned out to be far more honest and revealing than retrospective reports, and Pink adapts it to forty random self-checks per week. Oblique cards and deliberate practice are separate tools: the cards pry open stuck thinking with cryptic prompts, while deliberate practice is Ericsson's painful, feedback-heavy method for improving performance.

assets.topic: The Big Question, the Small Question, and Webber's Card Pair
assets.visual_frame_description: A nightstand at bedtime holds three artifacts: a plaque engraved with a one-sentence life summary, a journal open to the question Was I better today than yesterday?, and two blank three-by-five-inch cards. A bedside lamp casts warm light over each as the player sorts them.
assets.player_mission: Classify each question and practice — the sentence question, the daily improvement question, and Webber's morning-and-night card pair — into its correct column.
key_concepts: Clare Boothe Luce told President Kennedy in 1962 that a great man is one sentence.
Abraham Lincoln's sentence: He preserved the union and freed the slaves.
Franklin Roosevelt's sentence: He lifted us out of a great depression and helped us win a world war.
Contemplating your purpose begins with the big question: What's your sentence?
The small question — Was I better today than yesterday? — is asked before sleep each night.
Small measures include learning ten vocabulary words, making eight sales calls, or writing four pages.

Paying above average is the separate Akerlof-Yellen strategy, and the addendum clarifies that unequal pay is fair when job demands or contributions differ.

assets.topic: Wide-Ranging, Relevant, Hard-to-Game Metrics
assets.visual_frame_description: A compensation consultant's dashboard at Meridian Medical Devices shows one giant quarterly sales number ballooning in red while smaller dials for customer satisfaction, new product ideas, and peer evaluations stay greyed out. A second screen shows a web of balanced metrics glowing green.
assets.player_mission: Predict where a single-number bonus plan drives a product manager's behavior, then choose the metric design that converts if-then rewards into now-that rewards.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: Performance metrics become less combustible when they're wide-ranging, relevant, and hard to game: a pay plan resting on a single quarterly sales number narrows focus and invites corner-cutting, while a varied metric set — current and future sales, company revenue, customer satisfaction, new product ideas, peer evaluations — transforms if-then rewards into now-that rewards. The payoff for reaching metrics should be modest, not massive.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are the compensation consultant at Meridian Medical Devices. Product manager Theo's bonus rides almost entirely on hitting next quarter's sales number. You watch the data: his new feature requests for the quarter after next have flatlined, he has stopped visiting two happy but slow-paying customers, and his team logs overtime re-negotiating deal terms to land bookings before the deadline.
assets.stage_1_question: What does Pink's metric analysis predict Theo's behavior will spiral into?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Narrowing: Theo won't concern himself with the quarter after this one, the health of the company, or whether the firm is investing in research and development — and nervous people in his position cut corners to reach quarterly goals, exactly the pattern in the chapter's product-manager example.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The CEO hands you two new pay plans: Plan A — salary plus a massive one-time bonus if the quarterly number beats plan by 20 percent; Plan B — salary plus modest targets across current-quarter sales, current-year sales, two-year company revenue and profit, customer satisfaction, new-product ideas, and coworker evaluations. You recommend one.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Plan B — varied metrics are harder to finagle, modest gains rather than massive payoffs are less likely to narrow people's focus or encourage the low road, and a range of measures reflecting the totality of great work transforms counterproductive if-then rewards into less combustible now-that rewards.
key_concepts: A pay plan resting on one quarterly sales goal makes a product manager ignore the quarters after it.
Nervous managers may cut corners to reach a quarterly goal.
Good metrics include sales, customer satisfaction, new product ideas, and coworker evaluations.
When metrics are varied, they're harder to finagle.
The gain for reaching metrics shouldn't be too large.
Modest payoffs are less likely to narrow people's focus or encourage the low road.
The right mix of metrics varies considerably across organizations.
Some people will find a way to game even the most carefully calibrated system.
A variety of measures can transform counterproductive if-then rewards into less combustible now-that rewards.
Effective organizations compensate people in ways that let them mostly forget about compensation.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests narrow-goal dynamics as presented in the book: single-number contingencies narrow attention and invite corner-cutting, while broad, moderate-stakes metric portfolios protect intrinsic engagement. Pink's evidence is the contrast between narrow and wide metric designs in the compensation chapter, grounded in Deci's warning that contingent money is most demotivating.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)

assets.topic: The Zen of Compensation: A Raise Conversation
assets.visual_frame_description: An HR conference room at Bluepeak Logistics: Deniz, the HR director, stands before a whiteboard showing a pay scale with the words fair base marked above the market line, while CEO Anya tosses a glossy perks catalog onto the table with a printing of a giant quarterly bonus trophy.
assets.player_mission: Redirect the CEO's pay redesign — base-pay cuts funding a giant bonus pool and a perks catalog — toward fair, slightly-above-average base pay that takes money off the table.
assets.scenario_setup: You are Deniz, HR director at Bluepeak Logistics, a 400-person courier network. CEO Anya is redesigning pay to light a fire: she wants to cut base salaries 8 percent to fund a giant quarterly top dispatcher bonus pool, add a perks catalog of office espresso machines and swag, and celebrate pay in every all-hands. You believe this will backfire. Your mission is to redirect the plan toward the Zen of compensation before Friday's board vote.
dialogue: Anya: Deniz, money is the language people understand. Shrink the base, supercharge the bonuses, and let's talk about salary at every all-hands.
Deniz: That's precisely backwards, Anya. Pink's reading of Deci: the more prominent salary, perks, and benefits are in someone's work life, the more they inhibit creativity and unravel performance.
Anya: So you want us to pay less? That can't be the Type I way.
Deniz: The Type I way isn't bargain-basement wages — it's the Zen of compensation: in Motivation 3.0, the best use of money is to take the issue of money off the table.
Anya: And the equity questions? If two dispatchers in adjacent hubs earn wildly different amounts, people notice.

Deniz: Internal fairness means paying people commensurate with their colleagues; external fairness means matching similar work at similar organizations. Getting equity right isn't itself a motivator — it's how we stop money from becoming a de-motivator.
Anya: So what makes people actually feel paid well?

Deniz: Two moves: pay a little above average — Akerlof and Yellen found it attracts better talent, reduces turnover, and boosts productivity and morale — and if we keep any metrics, keep them wide-ranging, relevant, and hard to game, with modest payoffs.
choices: Abandon the base-pay cut and bonus pool; set fair, slightly-above-market base pay, keep perks modest, and let money recede into the background so the work itself leads.
Keep the bonus pool but double the base cut to make the fire bigger — more cash on the table means more motivation.
Keep pay flat and invest the savings in an espresso machine catalog; perks are the modern salary.
Compromise: equalize everyone's pay to the same number so no fairness complaint can ever recur.
assets.theoretical_principle: The Zen of compensation: fairness and adequate base pay that takes money off the table
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 executes the chapter's plan: internal and external fairness, slightly-above-average base pay per Akerlof and Yellen, modest wide-ranging metrics, and compensation designed to disappear from attention — the condition under which people focus on the work itself. Choice 1 amplifies exactly the salience that unravels performance, choice 2 mistakes perks for pay, and choice 3 confuses equal pay with fair pay, which the book rejects outright.
key_concepts: In Motivation 3.0, the best use of money is to take the issue of money off the table.
The more prominent salary, perks, and benefits are, the more they can inhibit creativity and unravel performance.
Edward Deci: when organizations use rewards like money to motivate staff, that's when they're most demotivating.
Effective organizations compensate people so they can mostly forget about compensation and focus on the work itself.
The most important aspect of any compensation package is fairness.
Internal fairness: pay commensurate with colleagues; external fairness: pay in line with similar work in similar organizations.
Akerlof and Yellen found paying a little more than the market could attract better talent, reduce turnover, and boost productivity and morale.
Higher wages could actually reduce a company's costs.
High base pay does more for performance and commitment than an attractive bonus structure.
Wide-ranging, relevant, and hard-to-game metrics transform if-then rewards into now-that rewards.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue tests the Zen of compensation: fair, adequate, slightly-above-average base pay that takes the issue of money off the table so the work itself can motivate. The Akerlof-Yellen efficiency-wage finding and Deci's demotivation warning anchor the policy choices the player must steer through.

credibility.basis: Popular science synthesis (Deci & Ryan self-determination research)
